  Small businesses accumulate records every day: quotations, invoices, contracts, customer enquiries, employee information, supplier documents, emails and operational files.

  Keeping records organised helps a business find information when it needs it. Keeping everything forever, however, can create unnecessary storage, security and privacy risks. Deleting records too early can be equally problematic when the information is needed for tax, contractual, regulatory or other legitimate purposes.

  A records retention schedule provides a practical way to manage this balance.

  For a growing South African business, the objective is to identify which records exist, why they are kept, how long they need to be retained, who can access them and how they should be disposed of when retention is no longer justified.

  This guide explains how to establish a manageable system. It provides general operational information, not legal or tax advice.

  ## 1. Understand what a retention schedule does

  A records retention schedule is a documented set of rules for managing records throughout their lifecycle.

  It usually identifies:
  - The category of record.
  - The purpose for keeping it.
  - The person or role responsible for it.
  - The applicable retention rule.
  - The event that starts the retention period.
  - The approved storage location.
  - Access and protection requirements.
  - The method of disposal.
  - Any conditions that suspend disposal.

  This is different from a simple folder structure. A folder structure helps people locate records; a retention schedule explains how the records should be managed over time.

  The schedule also prevents staff from making inconsistent decisions. One person should not delete an old invoice because it appears unnecessary while another keeps unrelated customer information indefinitely simply because storage space is available.

  ## 2. Identify the records your business actually holds

  Start with an inventory of the records created, received and stored during normal business operations.

  Common categories include:

  | Category | Examples | Why the records may matter |
  |---|---|---|
  | Tax and finance | Invoices, receipts, accounting records, supporting documents | Tax obligations, financial reporting and audit trails |
  | Contracts and agreements | Signed contracts, variations, termination records | Evidence of agreed terms and obligations |
  | Customers | Quotations, orders, service records and correspondence | Service delivery, disputes and customer relationships |
  | Suppliers | Purchase orders, invoices and supplier agreements | Payments, procurement and contractual obligations |
  | Employees and contractors | Employment records, agreements and relevant correspondence | Employment administration and applicable obligations |
  | Operations | Procedures, registers, maintenance records and approvals | Consistent work and accountability |
  | Marketing | Enquiry forms, mailing lists and campaign records | Managing communications and applicable privacy obligations |
  | Technology | Access logs, backups, system records and security incidents | Continuity, troubleshooting and security |
  | Governance | Policies, decisions, approvals and formal business records | Accountability and evidence of decisions |

  The table is a starting point, not a complete legal classification. The records required and their retention periods depend on the nature of the business and the laws, contracts and circumstances that apply.

  Include electronic records as well as paper files. Relevant information may exist in email accounts, cloud storage, accounting platforms, messaging systems, shared drives and backup services.

  Do not collect extra copies of sensitive information simply to complete the inventory. Record the location and category of existing material without unnecessarily duplicating it.

  ## 3. Identify the reason each category is retained

  Before choosing a retention period, establish why the business needs the record.

  Possible reasons include:
  - Meeting a legal or regulatory obligation.
  - Supporting a tax return or financial record.
  - Fulfilling a contractual requirement.
  - Managing an ongoing customer relationship.
  - Demonstrating how a decision was made.
  - Responding to an audit, investigation or dispute.
  - Protecting the business's legitimate interests where retention is lawful and justified.

  Different reasons can produce different retention requirements.

  A document required for a tax audit should not automatically be deleted according to the same schedule as an outdated marketing draft. Equally, a customer's personal information should not be kept indefinitely just because the business might find it useful one day.

  Record the reason for retention in plain language. If nobody can explain why a category is kept, investigate before deciding to retain or dispose of it.

  ## 4. Check applicable legal and contractual requirements

  Retention periods should be based on the rules that apply to the particular record, not on a single number used for every document.

  For example, the South African Revenue Service's [record-keeping guidance](https://www.sars.gov.za/client-segments/record-keeping/) explains that records required under the Tax Administration Act generally need to be retained for five years from the submission of the relevant return in the circumstances described by SARS. Additional conditions can extend retention, including certain cases where a return has not been submitted or an audit or investigation is ongoing.

  That does not mean every document in every business must automatically be kept for five years. Other legal requirements, contractual obligations and the nature of the record can affect the applicable period.

  A business should check the rules relevant to its tax status, industry and record types.

  For personal information, the Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) also matters. Section 14 establishes a general principle that personal information should not be retained longer than necessary for the purpose for which it was collected or subsequently processed, subject to specified exceptions.

  The [Information Regulator's privacy notice](https://inforegulator.org.za/privacy-notice/) describes retention, secure disposal and circumstances in which information may need to be retained for longer, including legal or contractual reasons.

  These requirements need to be considered together. A business should not delete records that it is legally required to keep merely because a customer relationship has ended. It should also avoid retaining personal information without an appropriate justification once the relevant purpose and lawful retention grounds have ended.

  If the requirements are unclear or conflicting, seek advice from an appropriately qualified professional before setting a final rule.

  ## 5. Define when the retention period begins

  A retention period is only useful when staff know how to calculate it.

  The starting event may be:
  - The date a tax return is submitted.
  - The end of a financial or reporting period.
  - The date a contract terminates.
  - The completion of a transaction.
  - The end of an employment relationship.
  - The date a case or matter is formally closed.
  - The date a record is superseded.

  The appropriate trigger depends on the rule that applies to the record.

  Avoid vague instructions such as "keep for five years" when staff cannot tell which event starts the five-year period.

  For example, if a retention requirement is measured from submission of a tax return, using the invoice date as the starting point could produce an incorrect disposal date.

  Where the retention rule depends on several conditions, document the calculation method and identify the person responsible for confirming the disposal date.

  ## 6. Build a practical retention register

  A small business can begin with a spreadsheet or another controlled register. It does not necessarily need specialised records-management software.

  The register might contain:

  | Field | Example of what to record |
  |---|---|
  | Record category | Tax supporting documents |
  | Business purpose | Support submitted tax information |
  | Applicable rule | Relevant SARS requirement |
  | Retention trigger | Submission of the relevant return, where applicable |
  | Retention period | Period confirmed for that record category |
  | Record owner | Finance or administration role |
  | Storage location | Approved accounting archive |
  | Access restrictions | Authorised staff only |
  | Disposal method | Approved secure deletion or destruction |
  | Review status | Current, under review or suspended |
  | Notes | Audit, investigation or other hold conditions |

  Do not use the example categories or periods as a substitute for checking the actual rules.

  Keep the register itself controlled. It should identify where records are stored without exposing unnecessary personal information or credentials.

  Assign a named person or role to maintain the schedule. If the business is very small, the owner may perform that role, but the responsibility should still be explicit.

  ## 7. Separate routine disposal from a legal or business hold

  A record may reach its normal disposal date while still being needed for a specific reason.

  Examples include:
  - An active tax audit or investigation.
  - A dispute or legal proceeding.
  - A contract that requires the record to be preserved.
  - An unresolved customer claim.
  - An instruction from an authorised professional or authority.
  - A legitimate investigation into a security incident.

  Establish a hold procedure that suspends ordinary disposal when an authorised person identifies a valid reason.

  The hold record should specify which categories are affected, who authorised it, the reason and when it should be reviewed.

  Do not continue a hold indefinitely without review. Once the reason ends and no other retention requirement applies, the record should return to the normal retention process.

  If the business receives a notice concerning an audit, investigation or legal matter, do not delete potentially relevant records while the situation is being assessed.

  ## 8. Protect records while they are being retained

  Retaining a document does not mean that everyone in the business should be able to access it.

  Apply safeguards appropriate to the sensitivity of the records.

  For electronic records, consider:
  - Individual user accounts.
  - Appropriate access permissions.
  - Strong authentication.
  - Encryption where suitable.
  - Protected backups.
  - Secure sharing methods.
  - Monitoring of important access or changes.
  - Timely removal of access when responsibilities change.

  For paper records, consider:
  - Locked storage for confidential material.
  - Controlled access to filing areas.
  - Secure transport of documents.
  - Safe handling of printouts.
  - Procedures for collecting and storing records away from public areas.

  POPIA requires responsible parties to take appropriate, reasonable technical and organisational measures to protect personal information against risks such as loss, damage and unauthorised access.

  The Information Regulator's [Personal Privacy Principles](https://eservices.inforegulator.org.za/pps/principles.aspx) provide practical guidance on collecting necessary information, maintaining accuracy and protecting records.

  Businesses serving customers in Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and elsewhere should apply the same basic principles regardless of whether records are kept in a physical office, on a local computer or in a cloud service.

  ## 9. Plan for email, messaging and cloud storage

  Important records do not always arrive as formal documents.

  A customer may approve a quotation by email. A supplier may confirm a change through a business messaging account. A contract variation may be recorded in a project platform.

  Decide which communications must be preserved as business records and how they should be transferred into an approved storage location.

  Avoid relying on one employee's personal inbox or phone as the only source of an important business record.

  Where cloud services are used, confirm:
  - Who administers the account.
  - Which records are stored there.
  - Whether the service supports export or retrieval.
  - How backups and deleted items are handled.
  - What happens when an employee or supplier leaves.
  - How records are disposed of when the retention period ends.

  Deleting a file from one folder may not remove copies in email archives, synchronised devices, shared locations or backup systems.

  For personal information, consider how the business and its service providers will manage retention and disposal across the systems involved. Do not assume that a cloud provider's default deletion process automatically satisfies every applicable requirement.

  ## 10. Decide how records will be disposed of securely

  When a record is no longer required and no retention obligation or hold applies, use a disposal method appropriate to its format and sensitivity.

  **Paper records:** Confidential documents may need secure shredding or an approved destruction service. Ordinary recycling is not appropriate for records that could expose personal, financial or confidential business information.

  **Electronic files:** Use the system's approved deletion process and consider whether copies exist in shared folders, devices, email archives or backups.

  **Portable devices:** Before disposing of or transferring computers, storage devices and removable media, ensure that information is handled using an appropriate secure-erasure or destruction process.

  **Third-party services:** Confirm how service providers handle retained copies and backups, and document any limitations or timelines that affect disposal.

  The method should reflect the risk. An outdated public brochure does not require the same treatment as a file containing identity documents, financial information or employee records.

  Keep a disposal log for categories where evidence of destruction is important. It may record the category, disposal date, method, responsible person and approval.

  Avoid placing unnecessary copies of sensitive information in the disposal log itself.

  ## 11. Review the schedule when the business changes

  A retention schedule should be reviewed when relevant laws, contracts, systems or business activities change.

  Triggers may include:
  - Introducing a new service.
  - Starting to collect a new type of personal information.
  - Changing accounting or payroll software.
  - Moving records to a new cloud provider.
  - Changing the company's legal or tax circumstances.
  - Entering a new regulated activity.
  - Discovering that records are being kept longer than intended.
  - Identifying a new audit, dispute or investigation requirement.

  A periodic review can also identify categories that have no owner, unclear retention triggers or unsuitable storage arrangements.

  Keep the review proportionate to the size and risk of the business. A small business may begin with a simple annual review and additional checks when significant changes occur.

  The important point is that the schedule remains aligned with actual business practices and applicable requirements.

  ## 12. A simple implementation plan

  You can introduce a retention schedule in manageable stages.

  **Week 1: Inventory**
  
  List the major categories of paper and electronic records, their storage locations and the people responsible for them.

  **Week 2: Confirm the rules**
  
  Identify the legal, tax, contractual and operational requirements that apply to each category. Verify retention periods with official guidance or qualified advisers where needed.

  **Week 3: Draft the schedule**
  
  Record the retention trigger, period, owner, access requirements and disposal method. Identify categories that need specialist review before a rule is approved.

  **Week 4: Approve and implement**
  
  Approve the schedule, communicate responsibilities, identify existing records that require review and establish a process for holds and disposal.

  This is an illustrative implementation timetable, not a statutory deadline. A business with extensive or sensitive records may need a longer project and specialist support.

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### Must every business record be kept for five years?

  No. SARS specifies retention requirements for relevant tax records, with conditions and exceptions. Other records may be governed by different legal, contractual, operational or privacy considerations. Confirm the applicable rule for each category.

  ### Can a business delete customer information when the customer relationship ends?

  Not automatically. The business should consider the purpose for which the information was collected, any applicable legal or contractual retention requirements, and other lawful grounds for retention. Dispose of information securely when retention is no longer justified.

  ### Should the business keep records only on paper?

  Not necessarily. SARS permits electronic record keeping in circumstances described in its guidance, subject to applicable requirements. Confirm the rules for your particular records and ensure that the records remain accessible and properly preserved.

  ### Is a spreadsheet sufficient for a retention schedule?

  It can be a practical starting point for a small business with a manageable number of record categories. More complex environments may need dedicated systems, formal approval workflows or specialist advice.

  ## Conclusion

  A records retention schedule helps a business preserve information it genuinely needs while avoiding uncontrolled accumulation of records.

  Start by identifying what you hold, why you keep it and which requirements apply. Then document retention triggers, access controls, holds, secure disposal methods and review responsibilities.

  For growing businesses in Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and across South Africa, a manageable records process can improve organisation and reduce avoidable operational risk.

  The schedule should reflect the business's actual circumstances. Confirm legal, tax, contractual and privacy requirements before approving retention periods or deleting records.

  A business website should do more than look professional. It should explain what a business offers, help potential customers decide whether it is suitable for their needs, and make it easy to get in touch.

  For a [small business](/articles/tag/small-business) in [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) or a surrounding community, the right website can provide a consistent place to present services, answer common questions and support enquiries outside normal business hours.

  The important question is not whether a website contains every modern feature. It is whether the website helps the right customer take the next step.

  ## 1. Start with a clear purpose

  Before choosing colours, animations or page layouts, decide what the [website](/services/web-development) must achieve.

  A local electrician may need customers to call or request a quotation. A tutor may need to explain subjects, schedules and lesson options. A retailer may need to display products and provide ordering information. A professional service provider may need to establish credibility before a prospect makes contact.

  These businesses have different needs. Their [websites](/articles/tag/websites) should reflect those differences.

  Start by identifying:
  - The main products or services.
  - The customers the business wants to reach.
  - The questions customers ask before buying.
  - The action visitors should take next.
  - The information that must remain accurate.

  The South African Government Communication and Information System's [website development guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/develop-revamp) emphasises planning, content and [accessibility](/articles/tag/accessibility) before development begins. Although written for government websites, these principles are useful for businesses too.

  ## 2. Make mobile usability a priority

  Customers may discover a business while travelling, comparing services on a phone or asking for a recommendation in a messaging group. A website should work properly on a smaller screen, not merely shrink a desktop layout.

  A practical mobile-friendly website needs:
  - Readable text without unnecessary zooming.
  - Menus that are easy to open and understand.
  - Buttons with enough space to tap accurately.
  - Forms that are comfortable to complete on a phone.
  - Images sized appropriately for the screen.
  - Contact details that are easy to find.

  This matters across Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and nearby areas, where customers may use different devices, network conditions and data budgets.

  [Mobile-first development](/services/web-development) also means testing the complete experience on a real phone. A page can technically fit a small screen while still being difficult to use.

  ## 3. Build pages around your services

  A homepage should introduce the business, but it should not be expected to explain everything.

  A small business website may need:
  - **Home:** A concise introduction and the main next step.
  - **Services:** An overview of what the business does.
  - **Individual service pages:** Details about important services, who they suit and what customers can expect.
  - **About:** Relevant experience, working approach and business background.
  - **Contact:** Accurate contact details and a straightforward enquiry option.
  - **Frequently asked questions:** Answers to recurring customer concerns.

  Not every business needs all these pages immediately. A simple business might start with a [focused one-page website](/promotions/mogen-seed-r99) and expand as its needs grow.

  Avoid creating empty pages simply to make a website appear larger. Each page should answer a real customer question or support a meaningful business task.

  ## 4. Explain the offer in plain language

  Visitors should not have to decode vague marketing language to understand what a business does.

  Instead of saying "We deliver innovative solutions", explain the actual service, its intended customer and the problem it addresses.

  For example, a plumbing business serving [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve) might explain the repairs it handles, its service area, how customers request quotations and whether emergency work is available. A consultant working with businesses in [Centurion](/locations/centurion) might describe the types of projects accepted and how an initial discussion works.

  These are examples, not claims that every business provides these services.

  Clear content helps customers assess suitability before making contact. It also reduces repetitive questions and mismatched enquiries.

  ## 5. Make contact straightforward

  A website can attract attention and still fail if visitors cannot work out how to proceed.

  Depending on the business, useful contact options may include:
  - A telephone link.
  - A WhatsApp enquiry link.
  - An email address.
  - A short enquiry form.
  - A booking or quotation request.
  - A physical address, where customers can genuinely visit.

  Each option should have a purpose. Do not add a complicated form when a simple enquiry will do.

  Forms should request only information needed to respond. Explain what happens after submission, show validation errors clearly and provide a confirmation when the enquiry has been received.

  If the business serves multiple areas, state the service coverage accurately. [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) and their surrounding areas should only be listed where the business can genuinely serve customers.

  ## 6. Prioritise speed and dependable performance

  Heavy images, unnecessary scripts, oversized videos and poorly configured third-party tools can make a website slow.

  A practical development process should include:
  - Resizing and compressing images.
  - Using appropriate modern image formats.
  - Loading non-essential media only when needed.
  - Avoiding unnecessary plugins and scripts.
  - Testing pages on mobile devices and slower connections.
  - Monitoring performance after updates.

  The [GCIS website and content-management guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/cms) specifically highlights responsive design, image optimisation, caching and performance on low-bandwidth connections.

  Speed is not simply a technical score. It affects whether a visitor can read information, complete a form or reach the business without frustration.

  ## 7. Design for accessibility and trust

  Accessible websites are easier for more people to use. Clear headings, sufficient colour contrast, meaningful link labels, descriptive image alternatives and keyboard-friendly navigation are useful foundations.

  Trust also depends on accurate business information. Use genuine photographs where possible, explain your process, publish realistic service expectations and make contact details consistent.

  Do not invent testimonials, certifications, client logos or project examples. If the business is new, explain its approach honestly rather than manufacturing a history it does not have.

  The [GCIS accessibility guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/website-accessibility) discusses text alternatives, understandable content and predictable interactions. These principles are valuable for commercial websites as well.

  ## 8. Make room for growth without overbuilding

  A new business does not necessarily need customer accounts, a database, an online store or a custom management system on day one.

  Begin with the features that support the current business model. Add more advanced functionality when there is a clear reason for it.

  A useful progression might be:
  1. Publish the essential business information.
  2. Improve service descriptions and enquiry handling.
  3. Add useful content and supporting pages.
  4. Introduce bookings, payments or integrations where needed.
  5. Automate repetitive tasks once the process is understood.

  This avoids paying for complexity before the business can benefit from it.

  ## 9. Local relevance needs genuine information

  A website serving [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka) should describe the services genuinely available to customers there. A business serving [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve) may need to clarify which extensions or nearby communities it covers. A business serving [Centurion](/locations/centurion) may need to explain its operating area, appointment arrangements or delivery coverage.

  Useful local content answers practical questions. It should not simply repeat town names throughout every paragraph.

  If a business has legitimate premises or distinct [service locations](/locations), its [website](/services/web-development) can provide accurate location details and explain what customers can expect at each one. Do not imply that a business has an office in an area where it does not operate.

  ## 10. Use a pre-launch checklist

  Before publishing, check that:
  - The website works on desktop and mobile.
  - Every important link and form functions.
  - Service descriptions and prices, where displayed, are accurate.
  - Contact information is correct.
  - Images are appropriately sized and have useful alternatives.
  - Pages have descriptive titles and headings.
  - Privacy information is available where appropriate.
  - The site uses HTTPS.
  - A backup and maintenance plan exists.
  - The business knows who is responsible for future updates.

  Google's [Search Essentials](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/essentials) and the [SEO Starter Guide](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/seo-starter-guide) provide further guidance on making useful, discoverable website content. Search visibility should support the website's purpose, not replace it.

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### How much website does a small business need?

  Enough to explain its offer, answer important questions and help customers take action. A focused one-page website can be a sensible starting point, while businesses with several distinct services may benefit from individual pages.

  ### Should a website mention Maboloka, Soshanguve and Centurion?

  Only where those locations are relevant to the business's genuine service area. Accurate location information is more useful than a long list of places the business cannot serve.

  ### Is a website still useful if the business uses social media?

  Yes. Social media can help people discover a business and begin conversations, while a website offers a more structured place for service information, policies, enquiries and useful resources. The two can complement one another.

  ### What should be improved first on an existing website?

  Start with the issues most likely to prevent customers from understanding or contacting the business: broken links, unclear services, incorrect details, poor mobile usability, slow pages and unreliable forms.

  ## Conclusion

  A good small business website is not defined by how many effects or features it contains. It is defined by how reliably it helps customers understand the business and move forward.

  Whether your customers are in [Maboloka](/locations/maboloka), [Soshanguve](/locations/soshanguve), [Centurion](/locations/centurion) or nearby communities, focus on clear information, mobile usability, performance, accessibility and straightforward contact options. Build a sound foundation first, then expand when your business has a clear need.

  A social media giveaway can attract attention, introduce a business to potential customers and create an opportunity to engage an audience.

  But a giveaway is not automatically a successful marketing campaign simply because a post receives many comments or new followers.

  If the prize attracts people who have no interest in the business, the campaign may generate activity without creating lasting value. If the rules are unclear, participants may question the outcome. If the business collects contact details without explaining how they will be used, a short promotion can create longer-term trust problems.

  A well-planned giveaway starts with a business objective, transparent participation rules and a realistic plan for what happens after the winner is selected.

  This guide is for South African small and growing businesses, including businesses marketing to customers in Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and other communities. It provides general operational guidance, not legal advice. The legal requirements for a specific competition should be checked against the applicable legislation and regulations.

  ## 1. Decide what the giveaway is meant to achieve

  Before choosing a prize, define the purpose of the campaign.

  A giveaway might be intended to:

  - Introduce a new product or service.
  - Increase awareness among a relevant audience.
  - Encourage people to learn about an offering.
  - Generate interest in a seasonal promotion.
  - Reward existing customers.
  - Collect feedback about a product or service.
  - Introduce a business to a new local audience.

  These objectives are different, so they require different campaign designs.

  If the aim is to reward existing customers, an elaborate campaign to attract thousands of strangers may be unnecessary.

  If the aim is to introduce a new service, the prize and campaign message should be relevant to the people who might actually need that service.

  Write down the intended outcome before creating the post. Otherwise, it becomes difficult to decide whether the campaign worked.

  ## 2. Choose a prize that attracts the right people

  A popular prize can generate engagement, but popularity alone does not make it a good marketing choice.

  Imagine a local business giving away a high-value electronic device unrelated to its services. The prize may attract many entrants, but some may have little interest in the business itself.

  Compare that with a prize connected to the actual offering.

  A bakery might offer a relevant product bundle. A fitness business might offer an introductory service. A professional business might offer a clearly defined consultation or service voucher, provided it can deliver the promised benefit.

  The best prize depends on the campaign's purpose and the business's ability to fulfil the offer.

  Consider:

  - Whether the prize is relevant to the intended audience.
  - Its full cost to the business.
  - Whether the business can deliver it reliably.
  - Any delivery or redemption restrictions.
  - Whether the prize is available for the entire campaign.
  - Whether the offer could create unexpected operating costs.

  A prize should be attractive enough to encourage participation without undermining the campaign's economics.

  ## 3. Define success before launching

  A giveaway needs a way to evaluate its results.

  Possible measures include:

  | Objective | Useful measure |
  |---|---|
  | Reach a relevant audience | Reach among the intended audience, where platform reporting supports it |
  | Generate interest | Relevant visits to the website or offer page |
  | Encourage enquiries | Qualified enquiries attributable to the campaign |
  | Reward customers | Participation from eligible existing customers |
  | Increase awareness | Relevant audience growth and subsequent engagement |
  | Support sales | Attributable purchases or bookings, where measurement is available |

  Choose a small number of meaningful measures.

  A large number of comments is not necessarily evidence of commercial success. Some comments may be unrelated to the business, while some relevant customers may engage quietly and contact the business later.

  Establish a baseline where practical. Record what happened before the campaign and define how the result will be assessed afterwards.

  Avoid promising a specific increase in sales, followers or enquiries. Results depend on the prize, audience, campaign design, distribution and many other factors.

  ## 4. Write the rules before promoting the giveaway

  Participants should understand the conditions before they enter.

  Prepare the rules before publishing the announcement. The post can summarise the main terms and direct people to a complete version where appropriate.

  Depending on the campaign, the rules may need to explain:

  - Who is organising the promotion.
  - What the prize includes.
  - Who is eligible to participate.
  - Where participation is available.
  - When the competition opens and closes.
  - How an entry is submitted.
  - Whether entry limits apply.
  - How the winner will be selected.
  - When and how the winner will be contacted.
  - What happens if the winner cannot be reached.
  - How and when the prize will be delivered or redeemed.
  - Any material restrictions or exclusions.
  - How personal information will be handled.

  The rules should reflect the actual campaign. Do not publish conditions that the business cannot honour or leave important decisions open to interpretation.

  In South Africa, section 36 of the [Consumer Protection Act 68 of 2008](https://www.gov.za/sites/default/files/32186_467.pdf) addresses promotional competitions within its defined scope. Applicable requirements can depend on the nature of the promotion and the relevant legislation and regulations.

  Do not assume that every online giveaway is legally identical or that a social media post alone satisfies every applicable requirement. If the promotion involves a significant prize, chance-based selection, unusual conditions or uncertainty about the applicable rules, obtain appropriate legal guidance before launch.

  ## 5. Make participation straightforward

  A campaign should explain what a participant needs to do without forcing them through unnecessary steps.

  If the entry method is to answer a question in the comments, state the question clearly. If entries must be submitted through a form, explain where the form is located and what information is required.

  Avoid introducing complicated requirements simply to increase activity.

  A long sequence of mandatory actions can confuse participants and make it harder to verify entries fairly.

  If the campaign is running on a social platform, review that platform's current promotion policies before deciding which entry methods to use. Platform requirements can change, and a campaign that works on one service may not be appropriate for another.

  Also consider accessibility. Use readable text, explain the entry process in the caption and avoid relying exclusively on information embedded in an image.

  A straightforward process helps participants understand the campaign and helps the business administer it consistently.

  ## 6. Be transparent about selection and the winner

  A giveaway can lose credibility if participants do not understand how the winner will be selected.

  Explain the method in advance.

  If the winner will be chosen randomly, establish a consistent process for identifying eligible entries and conducting the draw. If the winner will be selected based on skill or judged criteria, define those criteria before entries are assessed.

  Keep an appropriate record of the process.

  After the selection, follow the published rules. Do not change the criteria because a preferred participant did not win or because the business wants a different marketing outcome.

  Communicate with the winner through a reliable channel and explain the steps required to claim the prize.

  Be cautious of impersonation and fraudulent accounts. If a campaign attracts attention, scammers may attempt to contact participants while pretending to represent the business.

  Tell participants which account or channel will be used for official communication. Do not ask winners to provide unnecessary sensitive information or make unexpected payments to claim a prize.

  The process should be fair, explainable and consistent with the terms announced at the beginning.

  ## 7. Protect participants' personal information

  A giveaway may involve names, social media account details, email addresses, telephone numbers or other personal information.

  Before collecting information, determine what is necessary for the competition and how it will be used.

  For example, the business may need contact details to notify a winner and arrange delivery. That does not automatically mean the same information should be added to a general marketing list for unrelated future campaigns.

  Separate the purpose of administering the giveaway from any proposed ongoing marketing activity.

  Consider the following safeguards:

  - Collect only information needed for a defined purpose.
  - Explain who is collecting the information and why.
  - Restrict access to people who need it.
  - Avoid requesting sensitive details unnecessarily.
  - Keep information in an appropriate system.
  - Establish suitable retention and deletion practices.
  - Obtain and record consent where required.
  - Provide an appropriate way to withdraw marketing consent where applicable.

  South Africa's Protection of Personal Information Act (POPIA) is relevant to the processing of personal information. The Information Regulator's [POPIA guidance and resources](https://inforegulator.org.za/popia/) include guidance on direct marketing and prescribed forms.

  Section 69 of POPIA addresses unsolicited electronic communications for direct marketing, subject to the applicable provisions and exceptions. Do not assume that entering a competition automatically gives a business unrestricted permission to send future promotional messages.

  Where the campaign includes an optional marketing subscription, make that choice clear and separate from the information needed to administer the competition. Confirm the appropriate legal basis and consent requirements for the intended use.

  ## 8. Match the giveaway to the customer's journey

  A giveaway should have a sensible connection to the next step you want an interested participant to take.

  For example, a campaign intended to introduce a service could direct participants to a page explaining that service. An existing customer appreciation campaign may focus on the relationship rather than attempting to generate immediate sales.

  Avoid making the entry process unnecessarily promotional. Participants should not have to navigate unrelated pages or receive a sales pitch simply to understand the competition.

  If the campaign directs people to the website, make sure the destination provides the information promised in the post.

  The landing page should explain the offer, relevant terms and any next step. Test the page on mobile devices and confirm that the link works.

  A campaign should feel like a coherent interaction with the business, not an isolated attempt to attract attention.

  ## 9. Prepare for questions and problems

  Before launch, decide who will monitor the campaign and respond to participants.

  Common questions may concern eligibility, closing times, entry confirmation, prize details and winner selection.

  Prepare consistent answers for the questions most likely to arise. Make sure the person managing the campaign understands the rules and has authority to handle routine issues.

  Establish what happens if:

  - The promotional post contains an error.
  - The prize becomes unavailable.
  - A participant disputes eligibility.
  - An entry cannot be verified.
  - The selected winner does not respond.
  - A fake account impersonates the business.
  - The platform removes or restricts the post.

  Do not invent a solution after a problem occurs if the rules already specify how it should be handled.

  If an important change becomes necessary, assess its legal and platform implications before communicating it. Do not quietly alter material conditions and expect participants to accept the change.

  ## 10. Plan what happens after the giveaway

  The end of the competition should not mean the end of the campaign's usefulness.

  After the winner has been selected and notified, review the results against the objectives defined before launch.

  Consider:

  - How many eligible entries were received?
  - Did the campaign reach the intended audience?
  - Which questions did participants ask?
  - Did the campaign generate relevant website visits?
  - Were any qualified enquiries attributable to the promotion?
  - What did the prize and administration cost?
  - Were there complaints or misunderstandings?
  - What should be changed next time?

  If people showed interest in a service, consider whether useful educational content or a relevant follow-up offer would help them make a decision.

  Do not automatically add all participants to a mailing list or messaging campaign. Follow the applicable privacy and direct-marketing requirements for any subsequent communication.

  Retain appropriate campaign records, including the published rules, key dates, selection process and outcome, in line with applicable legal and operational requirements.

  >
  > If you are planning a social media campaign and need help connecting the promotion to a wider marketing objective, explore Mogen's digital marketing service.
  >
  > [Explore Mogen Digital Marketing](/services/digital-marketing)

  ## 11. Use a pre-launch checklist

  Before publishing, confirm that:

  - [ ] The campaign has a defined business objective.
  - [ ] The prize is relevant and available.
  - [ ] The full cost of delivering the prize has been considered.
  - [ ] Eligibility conditions are clear.
  - [ ] The opening and closing dates are correct.
  - [ ] The entry method is understandable.
  - [ ] The winner-selection method is documented.
  - [ ] The rules reflect applicable legal requirements.
  - [ ] Current platform promotion policies have been checked.
  - [ ] The process for contacting the winner is defined.
  - [ ] Personal information is collected and handled appropriately.
  - [ ] Any future marketing consent is handled separately where required.
  - [ ] The promotional post and destination links have been tested.
  - [ ] Someone is responsible for monitoring and responding.
  - [ ] The campaign's success measures have been recorded.

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### Do social media giveaways guarantee more customers?

  No. A giveaway can attract attention, but the outcome depends on its relevance, audience, design and follow-through. Engagement should not be treated as proof of sales or long-term customer growth.

  ### Can I add every participant to my marketing list?

  Do not assume that participation authorises unrelated future marketing. Determine the applicable legal requirements, explain the intended use of information and obtain or record consent where required.

  ### Do I need written terms and conditions?

  The appropriate requirements depend on the nature of the promotion and applicable law. A clear written set of rules is a practical safeguard, and South African promotional competition requirements should be reviewed before launch.

  ### Should I choose a prize with the highest possible value?

  Not necessarily. A relevant prize may attract a more suitable audience than a more expensive but unrelated item. Choose a prize that supports the campaign objective and that the business can deliver responsibly.

  > **CTA — Discuss your campaign**
  >
  > If you want to connect a giveaway with your website, content and broader marketing activities, contact Mogen to discuss your business objectives and requirements.
  >
  > [Contact Mogen](/contact)

  ## Conclusion

  A successful giveaway needs more than an attractive prize and an engaging post.

  Define the objective, choose a relevant reward, publish transparent rules, use a fair selection process and handle participant information responsibly. Then evaluate the campaign against its original purpose rather than relying on likes and comments alone.

  For South African small businesses, a carefully planned promotion can create a useful opportunity to introduce an offering and strengthen customer relationships. A poorly planned one can create confusion, operational costs and avoidable disputes.

  Plan the entire customer experience before launching, check the requirements that apply to your promotion and make sure the business can deliver what it promises.

  When planning a business website, one of the most important decisions is how the website should work behind the scenes.

  Some websites mainly present information: what a business does, which services it offers, where it operates and how customers can make contact. Others need to manage products, bookings, customer accounts, changing stock levels or information stored in a database.

  These different requirements can influence how a website should be built.

  A static website can be an excellent option for a business that needs clear information and a reliable way to generate enquiries. A dynamic website may be more appropriate when customers need to interact with changing data or complete transactions. Many modern websites combine both approaches.

  The best choice is not necessarily the most technically sophisticated one. It is the approach that meets the business's actual requirements without introducing unnecessary complexity.

  This guide explains the differences, the trade-offs and the questions South African small businesses should answer before commissioning a website.

  ## 1. What is a static website?

  A static website serves pages that have generally been generated before a visitor requests them. The resulting HTML, CSS, images and other assets can often be delivered directly from a web server or content delivery network.

  Static does not mean that the website must look plain or contain no interactive features. A static site can have sophisticated layouts, animations, navigation, enquiry forms connected to external services and other functionality.

  The defining characteristic is how the page content is generated and delivered, not whether the website looks modern.

  Consider a local service business that needs pages for:

  - Its services.
  - Its business background.
  - Areas it genuinely serves.
  - Frequently asked questions.
  - Customer testimonials, where appropriately obtained.
  - Contact details and an enquiry form.

  If the information changes occasionally and visitors do not need personalised accounts or database-driven transactions, a predominantly static architecture may be suitable.

  Updates still need to be made when information changes. Depending on the technology, that may involve editing content in a repository, using a content management system or rebuilding and redeploying the website.

  Static delivery can reduce the amount of server-side application processing required for ordinary page requests. However, the final cost, performance and maintenance requirements depend on the complete implementation.

  ## 2. What is a dynamic website?

  A dynamic website generates or updates content using application logic, data sources or other services.

  For example, an online shop may need to retrieve product information, calculate prices, manage stock, process orders and display order histories. A booking platform may need to check availability, reserve time slots and prevent conflicting bookings.

  These tasks require more than displaying fixed information.

  Depending on the architecture, a dynamic website may use:

  - A database.
  - A server-side application.
  - APIs that exchange information with other systems.
  - User authentication and permissions.
  - Background processing.
  - Payment or booking integrations.
  - Administrative interfaces.

  Not every dynamic website needs all these components. A relatively simple website can use a hosted booking service, for example, instead of implementing its own booking engine.

  The important question is whether the business needs information to be created, retrieved or changed through application logic.

  Dynamic functionality is valuable when it solves a genuine operational problem. It becomes a burden when it is introduced without a clear purpose.

  ## 3. Static vs dynamic vs hybrid websites

  The following comparison provides a starting point.

  | Consideration | Static website | Dynamic website | Hybrid website |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Typical content | Mostly informational pages | Frequently changing or personalised information | Informational pages plus selected dynamic features |
  | Data storage | May not require a website database | Often uses a database or external data service | Depends on the dynamic features |
  | Content updates | May require a rebuild, deployment or CMS workflow | May be updated through an application or administration interface | Different update methods may coexist |
  | Customer accounts | Usually unnecessary without additional services | Can support accounts and permissions | Can support accounts within selected parts |
  | Transactions | Usually handled through external services or added functionality | Can support custom transaction workflows | Can combine static pages with transactional features |
  | Maintenance | Depends on code, dependencies and connected services | May involve application, database and infrastructure maintenance | Requires clear ownership of each component |
  | Suitable examples | Brochure websites, service pages and information sites | Custom portals, inventory systems and transaction-heavy applications | Business websites with booking, search or selected interactive services |

  These categories are not mutually exclusive in every technical implementation.

  The [MDN Web Docs explanation of server-side rendering](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/SSR) notes that rendering approaches can be combined and distinguishes content generated at build time from content generated in response to a request.

  In practice, many modern websites use a hybrid architecture. Some pages are generated ahead of time, while other pages or components retrieve changing information when needed.

  ## 4. When is a static website the better choice?

  A static approach is worth considering when the main purpose of the website is to communicate information and generate enquiries.

  ### Your content changes infrequently

  If your service descriptions, business information and contact details change only occasionally, a complex administration system may not be necessary.

  You still need a reliable update process. The question is whether that process needs to involve a database and a full application backend.

  ### You need a clear customer journey

  Many small businesses need visitors to understand the service, evaluate whether it is relevant and contact the business.

  A well-structured website can support this journey with service pages, useful information, clear calls to action and a straightforward enquiry path.

  Those outcomes do not automatically require a custom database.

  ### You want to limit unnecessary complexity

  Every additional system introduces responsibilities.

  A database needs suitable access controls and backup arrangements. An application backend may need security updates and monitoring. A third-party integration may have its own subscription, configuration and failure conditions.

  If a business does not need these components, avoiding them can simplify the maintenance process.

  This does not mean static websites are automatically secure, maintenance-free or inexpensive. Dependencies, deployment systems, forms and external integrations still need appropriate management.

  ### You want a website that can grow in stages

  A small business does not have to build every possible future feature on launch day.

  It can start with the essential pages and enquiry process, then add functionality when there is a demonstrated business need.

  This staged approach works best when the original architecture and development agreement make future changes practical.

  ## 5. When does a dynamic website make more sense?

  Dynamic functionality becomes more valuable when the website needs to do work rather than simply present information.

  ### Customers need to manage accounts

  If customers must sign in, update their profiles, view private information or manage their own transactions, the website needs an appropriate way to identify users and control access.

  This introduces security and privacy responsibilities that must be designed deliberately.

  ### Your business manages changing data

  A catalogue with frequently changing stock, a booking system with live availability or a service portal with changing records may benefit from a database-backed application.

  A business with only a small number of products may not need a custom platform. A hosted e-commerce solution could provide the required functionality with less development work.

  The appropriate option depends on the business's processes, transaction volume, integrations and budget.

  ### You need automated workflows

  Some businesses benefit from systems that receive information, validate it, update records and trigger further actions.

  Examples include a customer submitting an application, a booking being confirmed or an order moving through different fulfilment stages.

  When these workflows are important, a suitable dynamic system may reduce manual work and improve consistency.

  Before building custom functionality, check whether an established service already meets the requirement. Reimplementing a common capability can create avoidable maintenance and security obligations.

  ## 6. The hybrid option: a practical middle ground

  A hybrid website combines different rendering and application approaches.

  A business could have mostly pre-generated service pages while using a separate service for bookings, payments or customer enquiries.

  Another implementation might generate public pages ahead of time but use server-side application logic for personalised sections.

  This can provide a useful balance between straightforward content delivery and the features the business actually needs.

  For example, a professional service business serving customers in Maboloka, Soshanguve or Centurion might need a public website with service descriptions and a contact form. If it later needs appointment booking, it could integrate an appropriate booking system rather than rebuilding the entire website around a custom backend.

  The choice should be based on how the components work together, including their costs, data handling, security responsibilities and failure modes.

  Hybrid architecture is not automatically the best choice, either. It may introduce additional services and integration points. Those dependencies should be documented and maintained.

  ## 7. Compare the total cost, not just the initial quote

  A website's cost includes more than the initial development fee.

  Consider the following categories.

  | Cost area | Questions to ask |
  |---|---|
  | Initial development | What pages, features and integrations are included? |
  | Hosting | Which services are required, and how are they billed? |
  | Content updates | Who can update information, and what does that work cost? |
  | Maintenance | Who handles updates, errors and technical changes? |
  | Security | What access controls, monitoring and recovery arrangements are needed? |
  | Integrations | Are there recurring fees or usage limits? |
  | Future development | Can the website be extended without replacing major components? |
  | Handover | What source code, documentation, accounts and operational information will be provided? |

  A static site may have low infrastructure requirements, but its content workflow may still need development support. A dynamic website may provide valuable automation, but the ongoing cost of maintaining that capability must be considered.

  Ask for the actual scope and recurring responsibilities rather than assuming that one architecture is always cheaper.

  ## 8. Do not overlook performance and search visibility

  Architecture influences how a website delivers content, but it does not guarantee search performance.

  A static site can still have oversized images, poor navigation, inaccessible controls or weak content. A dynamic site can be fast and search-friendly when it is implemented correctly.

  Google provides a [developer's guide to making websites search-friendly](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/get-started-developers). It explains that developers should consider crawlable links, sitemaps, how JavaScript content is rendered, security, performance, accessibility and support for different devices.

  If your website relies heavily on JavaScript, check that important content is available to search engines as intended and that key pages have discoverable URLs.

  Use normal links that crawlers can follow, make important pages reachable from other relevant pages and ensure that the website does not unintentionally prevent indexing.

  Performance should be assessed on the actual website rather than inferred from the label "static" or "dynamic".

  >
  > Planning a new website? Explore Mogen's web development service to discuss the pages, functionality and maintenance arrangements appropriate to your business.
  >
  > [Explore Mogen Web Development](/services/web-development)

  ## 9. Questions to answer before choosing an architecture

  Before approving a proposal, answer these questions with your developer.

  1. What must the website help the business achieve?
  2. Which information needs to change frequently?
  3. Will visitors need individual accounts?
  4. Will the website store or process customer data?
  5. Does the business need bookings, payments or other transactions?
  6. Can an existing third-party service provide the required functionality?
  7. Who will update the website after launch?
  8. Who is responsible for hosting, security and backups?
  9. What will the ongoing costs be?
  10. What happens if the business changes developers?

  The answers should lead to a defined scope. Avoid paying for functionality merely because it sounds impressive or because a particular technology is popular.

  If future requirements are uncertain, distinguish essential launch features from optional improvements. This allows the business to make a deliberate decision about when additional complexity becomes worthwhile.

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### Is a static website suitable for a small business?

  Yes, when its primary purpose is to present information and support enquiries. It can also connect to external services for selected interactive features. The suitability depends on the requirements, not the size of the business alone.

  ### Can a static website have a contact form?

  Yes. A form can submit information to an external form service or an appropriate backend. The form still needs reliable delivery, spam controls, privacy safeguards and a way to confirm that submissions are received.

  ### Is a dynamic website always more expensive?

  Not necessarily. Costs depend on the required features, platform, development approach and ongoing maintenance. A hosted service may provide dynamic functionality more economically than a custom implementation.

  ### Can a static website become dynamic later?

  Often, yes. The changes required depend on the original architecture and the new functionality. Discuss likely future requirements early so that the initial implementation does not create unnecessary barriers.

  ### Which type of website is better for SEO?

  Neither type guarantees better rankings. Both can support search visibility when their content, technical implementation, accessibility, performance and site structure are handled appropriately.

  > **Discuss your requirements**

  >
  > [Contact Mogen](/contact)

  ## Conclusion

  Static, dynamic and hybrid websites can all be suitable choices for South African small businesses.

  A static approach can work well when the website primarily communicates information. Dynamic functionality becomes useful when the business needs to manage changing data, customer accounts or transactions. Hybrid architecture can combine the two where that combination solves a genuine problem.

  The best decision begins with business requirements, not technology trends. Define what customers need to do, what the business must maintain and what the website will cost over time.

  Choose the simplest approach that meets those requirements reliably, while keeping future development practical.

  Choosing how to build a website is one of the most important decisions a growing business can make. The technology affects the initial development effort, ongoing maintenance, content updates, hosting requirements and the features that can be added later.

  It is easy to assume that a more sophisticated website is automatically better. In practice, a business may need only a handful of informative pages and a reliable enquiry form. Another business may need a publishing workflow, customer accounts, online payments or an application that manages complicated processes.

  The right solution is the one that meets the business requirements without introducing unnecessary cost or complexity.

  For businesses serving Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and surrounding areas, that decision should also consider mobile access, available data, staff skills and who will maintain the website after launch.

  ## What are the three options?

  Although the terminology can overlap, three broad approaches help explain the choices.

  **A static website** serves pages whose content is prepared before the visitor requests them. The content may be stored in HTML files or generated from source files and data during a build process. A static site can still include interactive features through JavaScript or connected services.

  **A content management system (CMS)** provides an interface for creating, editing, organising and publishing content. Depending on the platform and configuration, content may be stored in a database and assembled into pages when requested, or published as static output.

  **A custom web application** implements business-specific workflows or interactive functions. It may include user accounts, permissions, databases, dashboards, bookings, integrations or other functionality beyond a straightforward information website.

  These categories are not mutually exclusive. A website can use a CMS to manage content, generate static pages for delivery and include a custom application for a particular service.

  The decision should therefore be based on what the business needs to do, rather than on the label alone.

  ## 1. When a static website makes sense

  A static website can be an excellent fit when the business mainly needs to explain its services, show contact details, answer common questions and encourage customers to enquire.

  Typical examples include:
  - A tradesperson's website.
  - A small consultancy's service pages.
  - A business introduction and contact website.
  - A campaign landing page.
  - A small professional portfolio.
  - A brochure-style website with relatively infrequent updates.

  Static delivery can reduce the number of server-side components required to serve ordinary pages. It can also make caching and content delivery straightforward when the site is designed and deployed appropriately.

  However, static does not mean maintenance-free. The project still needs a deployment process, domain management, HTTPS, backups of source material, dependency updates where applicable and testing of forms or third-party integrations.

  A contact form, for example, may depend on an external service or a server-side endpoint even when the rest of the website is static.

  ### Who should choose a static website?

  Consider this option if the business has a clear, relatively stable set of pages and does not need staff to publish content frequently through a visual editing interface.

  It may also be suitable when a developer manages updates and the business values a simple delivery architecture.

  A static website is not automatically the cheapest option in every circumstance. Custom development can require specialist time, and even small changes may depend on the developer if the content workflow is not designed for business users.

  ## 2. When a CMS makes sense

  A content management system becomes useful when the business needs to update information regularly without asking a developer to edit source code for every change.

  Examples include:
  - A company publishing articles or news.
  - A business maintaining many service pages.
  - A team updating product descriptions.
  - An organisation managing several contributors.
  - A website with draft, review and publishing stages.
  - A business that needs a structured content library.

  The South African Government Communication and Information System's [CMS guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/cms) discusses content publishing, accessibility, performance, security, governance and content lifecycle management. Although it is written for government departments and public entities, these considerations can also help private businesses evaluate their requirements.

  ### What a CMS should provide

  Do not judge a CMS only by how attractive its editing screen looks.

  Review whether it supports:
  - The content types the business needs.
  - Straightforward editing and previewing.
  - Appropriate user roles and permissions.
  - Drafting and publishing workflows.
  - Reliable backups and recovery.
  - Search-friendly page structures.
  - Accessible content and forms.
  - A practical process for updates and maintenance.

  The complexity of the CMS should match the complexity of the publishing process.

  A small company with one person editing a few pages may not need the same workflow as a publication with several editors and frequent updates.

  ### A CMS does not have to mean a traditional database-driven website

  Some CMS arrangements generate static pages from managed content. Others provide content through an application programming interface (API) to a separately developed website.

  A headless CMS separates content management from the presentation layer. This can give a development team more control over the website experience, but it also introduces integration work, deployment considerations and potentially additional services to manage.

  Choose this architecture because its advantages solve a real problem, not simply because it is a modern technical pattern.

  ## 3. When a custom web application makes sense

  A custom application is appropriate when the business needs users to do more than read pages and submit ordinary enquiries.

  Possible requirements include:
  - Customer dashboards.
  - Appointment and booking management.
  - Personalised account areas.
  - Workflow approvals.
  - Business-specific calculators.
  - Inventory or order management.
  - Integration with an existing business system.
  - Different permissions for staff, customers and administrators.

  A business might start with a normal website and later discover that its customers need a secure portal to view records or manage requests. At that point, an application may be more appropriate than repeatedly adding plugins or workarounds to a basic website.

  But custom applications have responsibilities that ordinary brochure sites may not have to the same degree.

  They can require authentication, authorisation, data validation, secure storage, monitoring, error handling, backups, dependency management and ongoing testing.

  The business must account for these responsibilities when planning the project.

  ### Do not build an application to solve a simple information problem

  If customers only need to read a service description and contact the business, an elaborate application is unlikely to add enough value to justify its complexity.

  Before approving custom functionality, ask what users will be able to accomplish that they cannot accomplish adequately through a simpler website.

  If the answer is unclear, document the customer journey before committing to the build.

  ## 4. Compare the options against business requirements

  The following table is a starting point, not a universal cost or performance ranking.

  | Requirement | Static website | CMS | Custom application |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Basic service information | Usually suitable | Suitable | Often unnecessary |
  | Frequent content editing by non-developers | Requires a suitable workflow or integration | Usually a strong fit | Depends on the implementation |
  | Articles and publishing workflows | Possible | Usually a strong fit | Possible but may require more development |
  | Customer accounts | Requires additional functionality | Depends on platform and extensions | Often suitable |
  | Business-specific workflows | Limited without additional services | Possible with extensions or integrations | Often a strong fit |
  | Ongoing maintenance | Source, deployment and integrations | CMS, extensions, content and hosting | Application, infrastructure, data and security |
  | Future expansion | Depends on the architecture | Depends on platform and integrations | Depends on architecture and implementation |

  A hybrid solution may be the best fit. For example, a business could use a CMS for articles, static delivery for public pages and a separate application for authenticated customer functions.

  ## 5. Consider the people who will maintain the website

  The development decision should include the business's ability to manage the website after launch.

  Ask:
  - Who will update text, images and prices?
  - Who will publish new pages?
  - Who will handle technical updates?
  - Who will respond if a form stops working?
  - Who controls the domain and hosting accounts?
  - Who can restore the website if something goes wrong?
  - What happens if the original developer is unavailable?

  A technically elegant solution can become a business problem if nobody can maintain it.

  For a business operating around Maboloka or Soshanguve, the availability of reliable internet and the staff's comfort with the chosen editing process may influence the decision. A business in Centurion with several staff members contributing content may have different workflow needs.

  These are planning considerations, not reasons to assume that a particular technology is right for every business in a particular town.

  ## 6. Check performance and accessibility requirements

  Whichever approach you choose, the finished website should be usable on phones, readable, accessible and reasonably efficient on the connections available to your customers.

  The [GCIS accessibility guidance](https://www.gcis.gov.za/guidelines/website/website-accessibility) discusses WCAG accessibility principles and practices such as keyboard access, readable content and appropriate alternatives for non-text content.

  Performance should be tested after implementation. The technology name alone does not prove that a website will be fast.

  Image sizes, JavaScript, hosting configuration, external scripts, caching and page design can all influence the experience.

  A good development process measures the actual result and fixes the bottlenecks that matter.

  ## 7. Plan for growth without building everything immediately

  A common mistake is to implement every imaginable future feature during the first release.

  Requirements can change, and a business may never need some of the functionality it initially considers essential.

  Instead, separate requirements into three groups:

  **Required for launch:** The features needed for the business to operate and for customers to complete the main journey.

  **Useful next steps:** Improvements that have a clear purpose but can wait until the basic website is working.

  **Possible future features:** Ideas that should be reconsidered when customer demand or operational evidence justifies them.

  This approach makes it easier to control scope and evaluate new requirements rationally.

  It does not mean that the architecture should ignore future needs. Important decisions about data ownership, integrations, security and content structure should be made deliberately, even when some features are deferred.

  ## 8. A practical decision checklist

  Before choosing a solution, answer these questions:

  - Does the business mainly need to publish information?
  - How frequently will content change?
  - Must non-technical staff edit content independently?
  - Are customer accounts or private records required?
  - Are payments, bookings or approvals part of the core workflow?
  - What data must the website collect and protect?
  - Which integrations are genuinely necessary?
  - Who will maintain the system?
  - What budget is available for ongoing support?
  - What must be possible at launch, and what can wait?

  If most requirements concern presenting information, start by evaluating a straightforward website. If publishing is frequent, investigate a suitable CMS. If the business requires structured transactions or complex workflows, assess whether an application is justified.

  > If you are planning a new website or reviewing an existing one, explore Mogen's website to learn more about its digital services and consider which development approach fits your business requirements.
  >
  > [Explore Mogen](/services/web-development)

  ## Frequently asked questions

  ### Is a static website always faster than a CMS?

  No. Static delivery can reduce some server-side work, but the finished experience still depends on images, scripts, hosting, caching and implementation. A well-configured CMS website can perform well, while a poorly built static website can still be slow.

  ### Can I add a CMS to a website later?

  Often, yes, but the effort depends on the original architecture, content structure and publishing requirements. Planning for likely changes can make later integration easier, although it cannot eliminate all migration work.

  ### Does a custom web application need a separate website?

  Not necessarily. An application can be part of the same website, operate under a separate subdomain or use a different presentation layer. The appropriate arrangement depends on security, hosting, routing and business requirements.

  ### Which option is best for a small business in South Africa?

  There is no universal answer. Choose according to the services offered, content workflow, customer requirements, maintenance capacity and budget. Local conditions matter, but they do not automatically determine the technology.

  ## Conclusion

  Static websites, content management systems and custom web applications solve overlapping but different problems.

  A simple website can be the right starting point for a business that mainly needs to explain its services. A CMS can make frequent publishing easier. A custom application can support workflows that ordinary pages cannot handle adequately.

  For businesses serving Maboloka, Soshanguve, Centurion and surrounding areas, the best choice is the one that helps customers and staff complete their tasks reliably while keeping maintenance manageable.

  Start with the business requirements, compare realistic options and build only the functionality that has a clear purpose.
